Title: A Case of Uncommon EGFR Exon 19 Deletion L747_T751del with In Cis K754E Mutation in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
PMID: 
Authors: 

Abstract
E746_A750del, the most common and predominant EGFR exon 19 deletion in non-small cell lung cancer, shows excellent sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. However, other uncommon EGFR exon 19 deletions show varying responses to EGFR-targeted inhibitors. L747_T751del is a rare EGFR exon 19 deletion, with uncertain clinical sensitivity to EGFR-targeted inhibitors. Additionally, K754E in exon 19 is another rare EGFR alteration with potentially damaging consequences and lack of established.drug response patterns. Limited research exists regarding the structure and implications of L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation both in exon 19 of EGFR and sensitivity prediction of K754E mutation to EGFR-targeted inhibitors. Herein, we presented a case of a non-small cell lung cancer patient harboring an uncommon EGFR exon 19 deletion L747_T751del with in cis K754E mutation. A 41-year-old male with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma received gefitinib as the first-line treatment. Following disease progression after one year, leptomeningeal metastasis developed. Subsequent osimertinib treatment at 80 mg or 160 mg doses once daily proved ineffective for intracranial disease control. The patient’s leptomeningeal metastasis symptoms progressively worsened during osimertinib treatment. Drug binding dynamics simulation indicated reduced binding activity of osimertinib to L747_T751del and K754E mutation sites as compared to other third- or second-generation EGFR-targeted inhibitors. This study provides the first comprehensive investigation of the L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation and its interaction with EGFR-targeted inhibitors, offering valuable clinical guidance for treating uncommon EGFR exon 19 mutations.

Case presentation
A 41-year-old male with no smoking history was diagnosed to have left pleural effusion in May 2020. A positron emission tomography-computed tomography scan in July 2020 identified a tumor (1.1 × 0.8 cm) in the upper lobe of the left lung (Fig. 1A), accompanied by left pleural metastasis, and multiple vertebral metastases. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination in July 2020 revealed no abnormalities. A subsequent single photon emission computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral rib metastases (Fig. 1B), along with multiple thoracic (Fig. 1C) and lumbar (Fig. 1D) vertebral metastases. According to the 8th AJCC/TNM staging system, the disease stage of the patient was classified as IVb (c.T1bN0M1c). Following pleural space drainage, malignant adenocarcinoma cells were detected. Subsequent left pleural biopsy confirmed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (Figs. 2A, B), with positive staining for the immunohistochemical biomarkers TTF-1 (Fig. 2C) and NapsinA (Fig. 2D). NGS was conducted on the pleural biopsy sample at Geneseeq Technology Inc. by using a 425-gene targeted panel. This analysis identified the presence of uncommon EGFR ex19del L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation [c.2240_2254delTAAGAGAAGCAACAT (p.L747_T751del); c.2260 A > G (p.K754E)] (Fig. 3B), together with other genomic alterations in CTNNB1, SMARCA4, PTPN11, APC, and TP53 genes.
In July 2020, the patient received gefitinib 250 mg once daily as the first-line targeted therapy. Both the thoracic and vertebral lesions were stable during the gefitinib treatment (Figs. 4A, B). In August 2021, the patient developed various symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lethargy, and neck discomfort. The neck, chest and abdominal enhanced computerized tomography scan showed no progressive disease, and brain enhanced MRI revealed no abnormalities. However, in August 2021, transcranial doppler examination indicated remarkably elevated intracranial pressure. The patient then underwent lumbar puncture, which revealed high intracranial pressure (510 mmH2O) and the presence of atypical cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (Fig. 5A). In August 2021, the patient experienced epileptic seizure and underwent ventriculo-peritoneal shunt for hydrocephalus. Given the clinical progressive disease of LM, osimertinib treatment was initiated in September 2021. Despite treatment with osimertinib 80 mg once daily as the second-line therapy, his ophthalmalgia and blurred vision worsened after one month. The patient then underwent two cycles treatment of chemotherapy with pemetrexed 500mg/m2 plus carboplatin area under the concentration-time curve (5.0), combined with the antiangiogenic agent bevacizumab (15 mg/kg) as the third-line therapy; however, his LM symptoms continued to deteriorate. A repeat lumbar puncture confirmed pathological LM based on the detection of adenocarcinoma cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (Fig. 5B). Subsequent NGS testing of the cerebrospinal fluid reconfirmed the EGFR ex19del p.L747_T751del and p.K754E complex mutation in exon 19, with no relevant drug-resistance mechanism. Based on the poor response to pemetrexed-based chemotherapy plus bevacizumab, alternative cytotoxic chemotherapeutics or angiogenesis inhibitors were unlikely to demonstrate superior activity against LM. We then decided to rechallenge the treatment with osimertinib. The patient resumed treatment with osimertinib 80 mg once daily from December 2021, combined with intrathecal administration of pemetrexed 30 mg and methotrexate 10 mg. Unfortunately, his blurred vision and neck discomfort aggravated during this treatment session; hence, the dose of osimertinib was increased to 160 mg once daily in February 2022. In March 2022, the patient reported bilateral lower limb numbness and further increase in neck discomfort. Brain and full spine MRI revealed strip enhanced lesions in the spinal meninges (Fig. 4C). The patient then underwent radiotherapy at the dose of 25 Gy/2.5 Gy/10f to control LM, and targeted therapy with osimertinib was continued at the dose of 160 mg once daily. In April 2022, despite stable pulmonary (Fig. 4D) and leptomeningeal (Fig. 4F) metastases, the patient developed peritoneal metastasis (Fig. 4E), with the presence of adenocarcinoma cells in the ascites (Fig. 5C). The patient ultimately discontinued the treatment against medical advice and died in July 2022.
